blocks.text: Sellowrap Industries Ltd makes small, customised plastic and foam parts and sells them business-to-business to car makers and their Tier-1 suppliers [F] (AR2026 p.7; SCREENER). The products are injection-moulded clips, grips, guide rails and air guides; polyurethane foam fenders and baffles; foam labels and stickers; door water shields and protective films; and, through a 26% associate, expanded-polypropylene (EPP) parts such as bumper cores and tool kits [F] (AR2026 p.13-15; PPT Jun 2026). Revenue comes from per-part prices on OEM vehicle programmes. Parts are developed against OEM drawings over 18-24 months and then supplied for the life of the model [MC] (CALL Jun 2026; AR2026 p.28). There is no aftermarket or distributor channel [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

FY26 consolidated revenue was Rs 200.82 cr (+23.6%), EBITDA Rs 26.21 cr including Rs 1.36 cr other income, and PAT Rs 10.13 cr including a Rs 1.21 cr share of associate profit [F] (AR2026 p.57, p.99). Our statements data shows TTM sales of Rs 218 cr, EBITDA of Rs 22 cr (10% margin) and PAT of Rs 9 cr [F] (NUMBERS). The latest quarter, Jun 2026 (Q1 FY27), had sales of Rs 59.86 cr (+39.5% YoY) but an EBITDA margin of only 6.33%, against 14.97% a year earlier [F] (NUMBERS).

Management says the top 5 customers are about 60% of revenue [MC] (CALL Jan 2026) and that the top 10 are 50-55% [MC] (CALL Jun 2026; AR2026 p.50). These two statements cannot both be true. Revenue by customer is not disclosed for any customer [F] (AR2026).

Listing status [F]: the company listed on NSE Emerge, the SME platform, on 1 August 2025 through a fresh issue of 36,48,000 shares at Rs 83, raising Rs 30.28 cr (AR2026 p.57). The evidence base is thin: one annual report, one half-yearly presentation, two investor calls hosted by the company's IR agency, and no prospectus in our materials [F]. The prospectus (RHP) was not available to us. The shareholder register held 348 shareholders in Sep 2026 [F] (NUMBERS).

blocks.text: Driver classification [AI]: theses 1 and 7 are cyclical, since they depend on auto volumes and commodity costs. Theses 3, 5 and 6 are company-specific. Thesis 4 is company-specific but rests on an undefined management metric. Thesis 2 is a valuation argument, not a business driver. Localisation and China-plus-one sourcing, which management cites, would be structural if it shows up in export revenue, but the foreign-exchange earnings data does not yet show it (AR2026 p.62).

items: 1. **Growth consumes more cash than it generates.** [F] Operating cash flow was -Rs 14 cr in FY26 against PAT of Rs 10 cr. Free cash flow was negative in 4 of the last 5 years, -Rs 39 cr in total over five years, and CFO/PAT was 0.46x over the same period (NUMBERS).

2. **Margins have collapsed in the latest data.** [F] EBITDA margin fell from 14.97% in Q1 FY26 to 9.07% in Q4 FY26 and 6.33% in Q1 FY27, while sales rose (NUMBERS). [MC] Management guided to 13-15% once costs normalise (CALL Jun 2026), but the price pass-through had only been requested, not agreed (CALL Jun 2026).

3. **The company lends to a promoter-linked food company, and its own disclosures about the loan contradict each other.** [F] Rs 3.70 cr is lent on demand to Prystine Foods And Beverages Pvt Ltd, where the MD is a director, and the company also holds Rs 1.50 cr of its unlisted equity (AR2026 p.66, p.77, p.90). [F] The auditor's CARO report calls the borrower an 'associate'; Note 41(x) says there are no such loans; the BRSR says loans to related parties are 'Nil' (AR2026 p.71, p.92, p.123). [E] The outstanding balance rose by about the same amount as the interest 'received', which implies the interest was accrued rather than paid in cash (AR2026 p.90).

4. **Key operating numbers disagree across the company's own documents.** [F] Capacity utilisation is given as 77% in the presentation and 85% in the annual report; export share as 23%, 17.43% (BRSR) and 3.7% on foreign-exchange earnings; customer concentration as top-5 at 60% but top-10 at 50-55%; units as 1.2 mn sold vs 118.6 mn produced (PPT Jun 2026; AR2026 p.7, p.51, p.62, p.119; CALL Jan 2026; CALL Jun 2026).

5. **The Rs 275 cr order book is undefined and has not moved.** [F] The same Rs 275 cr figure appeared in Jan 2026 and again in Aug 2026, although about Rs 114 cr of H2 revenue was billed in between (CALL Jan 2026; AR2026 p.6; PPT Jun 2026). [AI] Either new orders exactly replaced billings or this is a programme-lifetime estimate, not a firm backlog.

6. **The bear DCF case gives negative equity value.** [F] At 8% EBITDA margin and about 6% growth, FCFF is Rs 1.3-2.6 cr a year, EV is Rs 25.8 cr, and equity value is -Rs 14/share after Rs 45 cr of borrowings (NUMBERS). The equity carries real leverage to margins.

7. **Promoter-family costs are rising faster than the business.** [F] The MD's pay rose 50% to Rs 1.50 cr and directors' remuneration rose to Rs 2.64 cr. The spouse and son are on the payroll. The company finances Mercedes, BMW and other cars and carries a home loan. A new Rs 0.81 cr 'education sponsorship' expense appeared in FY26 (AR2026 p.62, p.79-81, p.87, p.90).

8. **Working capital is swelling.** [F] The cash conversion cycle widened from 90 to 117 days; inventory rose 46% and receivables 41%, against revenue growth of 24% (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.98). [F] The cash-credit line was drawn to Rs 14.21 cr of a Rs 15 cr sanction (AR2026 p.83).

9. **IPO capex money is idle while debt rises.** [F] Rs 12.40 cr of IPO capex proceeds sat in FDs at year-end, while long-term borrowings rose from Rs 14.67 cr to Rs 23.06 cr (AR2026 p.79, p.91). [MC] Deployment has been promised 'in 6 to 7 months' (CALL Jun 2026).

10. **The shares are illiquid and institutions are leaving.** [F] There are 348 shareholders. DII holding fell from 4.48% to 1.92% and FII holding from 4.11% to 3.67% between Sep 2025 and Sep 2026. The price is Rs 61.6, against the Rs 83 IPO price and a 52-week high of Rs 105 (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.57).

blocks.text: [AI] The market prices Sellowrap as a low-growth auto ancillary (the reverse DCF implies 6.9% growth, NUMBERS), even though revenue is compounding at 16-24%. On that narrow point, the bulls have it right. But they have the cause of the cheapness wrong. The stock is not cheap because the market is missing the growth. It is cheap because the growth has not produced cash (CFO -Rs 14 cr in FY26, NUMBERS), because margins fell to 6.3% in the latest quarter (NUMBERS), and because the documents contain contradictions in exactly the places an investor most needs consistency: related-party lending, export share, customer concentration, capacity and the order book (AR2026 p.62, p.71, p.90, p.92, p.119-123). Our variant view is that the re-rating trigger is not more revenue growth. It is (a) positive operating cash flow in H1 FY27, (b) EBITDA margin back above 10%, and (c) recovery or clean disclosure of the Rs 3.70 cr Prystine loan. Without these, the base DCF value of Rs 77.5 (NUMBERS) is not reachable on a risk-adjusted basis.

blocks.text: [AI] The business is old, about 40 years in Gurgaon foam and labels, but its current shape is recent. Ranipet, now about half of revenue, dates only from 2018. Pune dates from 2021. Revenue was Rs 58 cr in FY21 and reached Rs 200 cr in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS; PPT Jun 2026). In other words, roughly two-thirds of today's revenue has been built in the last five years on plants that are under eight years old. The listed-company history is 14 months long, with one audited annual report as a listed entity. The company's own account of its founding year (1983 vs 1985) and of when the EPP JV began (2005 vs 2011) is inconsistent [F] (AR2026 p.7, p.63; PPT Jun 2026), so even the basic history needs care.

items: 1. RFQ and nomination: the OEM or Tier-1 issues an RFQ, often through its global purchasing office in India [MC] (CALL Jan 2026).

2. Design and development: the company does Class-A surface design, CAE, mould-flow analysis and prototype tooling at its Pune, Ranipet and Gurgaon R&D desks, with 25 R&D staff [F] (AR2026 p.19-20). Validation projects worth Rs 1.34 cr were executed in FY26 for Renault, Nissan and Mahle [F] (AR2026 p.21).
3. Development cycle: 18-24 months from award to start of production [MC] (CALL Jun 2026; AR2026 p.28).

4. Raw materials: polymers (PP, PE, ABS, nylon, polycarbonate, PU chemicals, films, adhesives) are about 62% of COGS [MC] (AR2026 p.50, p.13). Imports were 13.12% of raw material consumed [F] (AR2026 p.89).

5. Conversion: 37 injection-moulding machines across 3 plants, an LDPE blown-film line, an adhesive coating line, foam cutting, ultrasonic welding, and in-house special-purpose machines and assembly lines [F] (PPT Jun 2026; AR2026 p.20).
6. Delivery: just-in-time supply from plants near OEM clusters. Domestic credit terms are 30-90 days; for 'export' supplies about 150 days from receipt [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).
7. Pricing: formula-based, annual and price-reduction contracts all exist; raw-material and FX recovery lags by 3-6 months [MC] (CALL Jan 2026; CALL Jun 2026).

blocks.text: [AI] Value is captured at two points. The first is design-in: once a part is validated on a vehicle programme, switching supplier mid-life is costly for the OEM [MC] (AR2026 p.29). The second is niche converting know-how in water shields and foam, where management claims mid-to-high-20s segment margins [MC] (CALL Jan 2026). Gross margin (revenue less material cost) was about 45% in FY25 and FY26 [E] (AR2026 p.75; PPT Jun 2026). Conversion costs are heavy, however: contract labour alone was Rs 14.53 cr and employee cost Rs 19.85 cr [F] (AR2026 p.87). That leaves EBITDA of 12-13%, in line with management's own description of OEM ancillary economics (CALL Jun 2026). The customer, not the supplier, captures most of the value, through annual price-down contracts [MC] (CALL Jan 2026).

[F] Contract workers were 502 of 530 workers in the BRSR, or 690 workers in the narrative section; contract labour cost Rs 14.53 cr in FY26, up 24% (AR2026 p.40, p.87, p.120). [MC] Management plans to fall back on nearby outsourcing if a plant is disrupted (CALL Jun 2026). [F] Fixed-asset turnover was 4.08x and capex/sales averaged about 7.5% over FY21-FY26 [E] (NUMBERS). [AI] On fixed assets the business is moderately asset-light, but on working capital it is heavy: a 117-day cash conversion cycle (NUMBERS). Working capital, not machinery, is what absorbs the cash.

blocks.text: [AI] Injection-moulded fasteners, labels, stickers and bought-out parts are commodity-like. Many Indian moulders can make them, and management itself calls part of the mix 'commoditised' [MC] (CALL Jan 2026). Water shields and engineered foams are the only lines with a credible claim to differentiation: a high claimed share, single-source status on some parts, and better margins [MC] (CALL Jan 2026; CALL Jun 2026). Even these are die-cut films and foams rather than proprietary technology, and the company discloses no patents or IP [F] (AR2026). Without the associate, about 50% of revenue is plausibly commodity-like and 45-50% is differentiated at best [E] (PPT Jun 2026).

[F] The audited accounts report a single segment, 'manufacturing and sale of auto parts', and no geographical segment (AR2026 p.78, p.91). Product splits exist only in presentations and the BRSR, and only for FY26. No three-year product series is disclosed [F] (PPT Jun 2026; AR2026 p.119).

blocks.text: Segment margins are not disclosed in any audited or written document. The only margin data is spoken figures from the Jan 2026 call, '16% to 17%, 21% to 23%', with no product labels [MC] (CALL Jan 2026). The Jan 2026 plant split (Pune 23%, Gurgaon 20%, Ranipet 49%) adds to 92% and does not reconcile with the FY26 presentation split [F].

items: Foam: [MC] growth credited to process know-how, 'nesting' and leading share in one or two products (CALL Jan 2026). [AI] Plausible, but foam utilisation is 71-74% at Pune and Ranipet against 90% at Gurgaon (AR2026 p.51-52), so the growth is concentrated in the oldest plant.

Injection moulding: [MC] demand strong; some plants at 90%, others at 60-75% (CALL Jun 2026). [F] Plastic injection utilisation is 93% at Ranipet and 94% at Gurgaon (AR2026 p.51-52). [AI] Injection moulding is the capacity bottleneck, which explains the machine orders.

Pune: [F] its revenue share rose from about 23% to 27.8% and its receivables nearly doubled, from Rs 6.47 cr to Rs 12.35 cr (AR2026 p.86; PPT Jun 2026). [AI] Pune is the main source of incremental growth and of the receivables build. Customer identity is not disclosed.

blocks.text: [AI] Every line is programme-driven. Revenue follows OEM production schedules on parts already nominated, so 'organic' here means volume on existing programmes and 'order-driven' means new programme starts. Management's 18-24 month development cycle (CALL Jun 2026) means FY27 revenue rests mainly on programmes won in FY25-FY26. None of these is named or quantified individually.

subsections.title: Is the export mix strategy or mix?

blocks.text: [AI] Most of what management calls exports appears to be 'deemed export': parts supplied to OEMs or their Indian units for vehicles or kits shipped abroad, paid in rupees. Management said in Jan 2026 that 'these all are deemed... deemed export' (CALL Jan 2026). Foreign-exchange earnings of Rs 7.35 cr (AR2026 p.62) imply true direct exports of only about 3.7% of revenue [E]. Export growth is therefore mainly a mix effect, driven by which OEM programmes are export-oriented (Nissan, Renault, JLR-linked work), not by the company's own overseas sales. The strategic claim that 40-45% of the Rs 275 cr order book is export (CALL Jun 2026) cannot be tested.

items: Currency: [F] foreign-exchange outgo was Rs 23.03 cr (raw material Rs 12.91 cr, machinery Rs 8.20 cr) against earnings of Rs 7.35 cr. [E] The company is a net foreign-exchange spender of about Rs 15.7 cr a year (AR2026 p.62, p.89-90). [F] The rupee moved from 85.53 to 94.71 per USD between Mar 2025 and Mar 2026 (PPT Jun 2026). [F] A foreign-exchange gain of Rs 0.13 cr was booked (AR2026 p.86). [F] No hedging policy is disclosed.

Tariffs: [MC] exports are to Europe and Asia, so direct US tariff exposure is minimal (AR2026 p.42; CALL Jun 2026). [F] The presentation lists North America and Mexico among export destinations, while the BRSR country list has no US entry (PPT Jun 2026; AR2026 p.119). Not reconciled. No tariff events with dates affecting the company are disclosed.

Geopolitics: [F] US-Israel strikes on Iran on 28 Feb 2026 disrupted Strait of Hormuz traffic, raising energy and polymer costs, per management's slide (PPT Jun 2026). [MC] The disruption was not resolved as of June 2026, and buffer inventory is still held (CALL Jun 2026).

Single location: [F] Ranipet is about 50% of revenue (AR2026 p.29; PPT Jun 2026). [MC] Production would move to other plants after customer approval, with some outsourcing (CALL Jun 2026; AR2026 p.41). [AI] Customer re-approval of transferred tooling takes time. Ranipet's 87% utilisation and the other plants' utilisation suggest limited spare capacity to absorb a transfer (AR2026 p.51-52).

blocks.text: [MC] Management describes competition by category: in plastics, large players such as Lumax and similar-sized players such as Radiant and PPAP; in foam, smaller converters (CALL Jan 2026). [F] The AR describes the sector as 'intensely competitive' with continuous OEM cost-down demands (AR2026 p.42, p.51). Without peer data in the evidence base, we use comparables only qualitatively: Sellowrap's 10-13% EBITDA margin is, by management's own account, 'quite in line with the ancillary suppliers' (CALL Jun 2026).

[AI] The landscape is fragmented, OEM-dominated and price-led. Sellowrap's defensible ground is narrow: water shields and engineered foam, where it claims leadership. Its injection-moulding business, now the largest line at 42.7-44.5% of revenue (AR2026 p.119; PPT Jun 2026), competes against larger, better-capitalised Tier-1s. summary.one_line: Sellowrap is a fast-growing, long-tenured OEM plastics-and-foam supplier trading at Rs 61.6, below its Rs 77.5 base DCF value but above a negative bear value.
